questions.question: The 87-lot ground truth is your own taps from one tapper over five days — what's your inter-rater reliability, and why not a held-out labeler?
questions.why: Slide 13 admits the truth set is one tapper's own taps with a 53–75% interval, a classic single-source-of-truth problem.

questions.question: Was top-3 chosen as the bar before you saw the top-1 numbers, or after top-1 came in lower than you wanted?
questions.why: Slide 13 quietly swaps the headline metric from top-1 to top-3 right after the top-1 gain is shown, which smells like a post-hoc bar.

questions.question: You show four different top-3 numbers from 70 to 82 percent — which one did you actually gate decisions on while running the experiments, in real time?
questions.why: The backup slide admits the four yardsticks disagree and says you can't draw one line through them, which undercuts every number shown earlier.

questions.question: What actually stops an unattended overnight agent from merging a change that passes its gate but is wrong in a way the gate didn't anticipate?
questions.why: The idle-tab-burning-a-day's-budget story on the gates slide shows the safety net already failed once silently.

questions.question: Letting the swarm self-steer broke the next day — what specifically did it do, and how do you know your fix wasn't just papering over the same failure mode recurring later?
questions.why: Slide 10 mentions this in one line with no detail on what broke or how it was caught.

questions.question: The persona panel said DONE at 21:50 and you found it unusable on your own phone the next morning — how many other DONE verdicts have you not personally re-checked?
questions.why: Slide 17 is a documented gate failure and the obvious follow-up is whether it's an isolated incident or systemic.

questions.question: Is the 'about 30 minutes a day' anywhere logged with timestamps, or is it entirely recall — and does it include the time spent writing gates and briefs, not just babysitting runs?
questions.why: The talk repeatedly flags this as 'my estimate, not a measurement,' which is exactly the kind of unverified labor claim that erases the human cost.

questions.question: The 45-forks estimate on the fork-tree slide is explicitly your own count and not in the record — how would that number change the ROI story if it were, say, half that?
questions.why: Slide 5 flags the grid as the speaker's own tally rather than mined data, which is a soft number dressed as structure.

questions.question: The language head's dev split for tuning its one knob — was that split drawn from the same distribution as the 201 test photos, or could it share sellers, listings, or lighting conditions with them?
questions.why: The backup slide's held-out defense addresses image leakage but not distributional leakage between dev and test splits.

questions.question: You raised the per-run caps from 8 calls and $6 to 14 calls after agents hit the wall — who signed off on that, and is there a hard ceiling above which an agent still can't spend more no matter what?
questions.why: Slide 11 mentions the cap increase as a bare fact with no governance detail, which matters for unattended-run safety.
